Unitary anchored planar algebras
André Henriques, David Penneys, James Tener

Abstract
In our previous article [arXiv:1607.06041], we established an equivalence between pointed pivotal module tensor categories and anchored planar algebras. This article introduces the notion of unitarity for both module tensor categories and anchored planar algebras, and establishes the unitary analog of the above equivalence. Our constructions use Baez’s 2-Hilbert spaces (i.e., semisimple C ∗ \rm C^{*} -categories equipped with unitary traces), the unitary Yoneda embedding, and the notion of unitary adjunction for dagger functors between 2-Hilbert spaces.



1
Introduction

Planar algebras were introduced by Vaughan Jones in
[
Jon21
]
.
A planar algebra
{\mathcal{P}}
is a collection of vector spaces
{\mathcal{P}}[n]
, called
box-spaces
, indexed by the nonnegative integers, along with a linear map

Z(T):{\mathcal{P}}[n_{1}]\otimes\cdots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[n_{k}]\longrightarrow{\mathcal{P}}[n_{0}]

for every planar tangle
T
. These maps are required to be compatible with the operation of composition of tangles in the sense that

Z(S\circ_{i}T)=Z(S)\circ(\id\otimes\ldots\otimes\id\otimes Z(T)\otimes\id\otimes\ldots\otimes\id)
.
See §
4.1
for more details.

In
[
HPT23b
]
, we internalised the notion of planar algebra to the context of a pivotal braided tensor category
{\mathcal{V}}
, and called the resulting notion an
anchored planar algebra
.
The box-spaces
{\mathcal{P}}[n]
of an anchored planar algebra are now objects of our ambient category
{\mathcal{V}}
, and we have morphisms

Z(T):{\mathcal{P}}[n_{1}]\otimes\cdots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[n_{k}]\longrightarrow{\mathcal{P}}[n_{0}]

for every anchored planar tangle. For example:

The full definition is given in §
4.2
.

We then proceeded to establish
an equivalence of categories

\left\{\,\text{\rm Anchored planar algebras in ${\mathcal{V}}$}\left\}\,\,\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{\,\parbox{128.0374pt}{\rm Pointed pivotal module tensor categories over ${\mathcal{V}}$}\,\right\}\right.\right.\!\!

between the category
\mathsf{APA}
of anchored planar algebras in
{\mathcal{V}}
, and the
category
\mathsf{ModTens}_{*}
of pointed
1
1

1

Here, “pointed” means equipped with a distinguished symmetrically self-dual object that generates the module tensor category.
pivotal module tensor categories over
{\mathcal{V}}
whose action functor admits a right adjoint.
We refer the reader to §
3.1
below for definitions of these notions.

In this paper we further specialise/generalise the notion of anchored planar algebra to the context when
{\mathcal{V}}
is a
unitary
pivotal braided tensor category, and we prove an analog of the above result.
This is motivated by enriched subfactor theory
[
JL17
]
, bicommutant categories
[
Hen17b
,
HP17
,
HP23
]
, topological orders
[
HBJP23
]
,
and higher unitary categories
[
CHPJP22
,
DHP22
]
.

Let
{\mathcal{V}}
be a braided unitary tensor category equipped with a unitary dual functor (the latter is the unitary analog of a pivotal structure
[
Yam04
,
Sel11
,
Pen20
]
; see §
2.2
below for more details).
A unitary module tensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
is called
pivotal
if it is equipped with a unitary dual functor, compatibly with the action of
{\mathcal{V}}
.
Our main result is the unitary analog of Theorem
[
HPT23b
, Thm. A]
:

Theorem A
.

There is an equivalence of categories
2
2

2

The 2-category of unitary pointed module tensor categories is equivalent to a 1-category. Moreover, the unique 2-morphism between two 1-morphisms, when it exists, is always unitary.

\left\{\,\parbox{128.0374pt}{\rm Unitary anchored planar algebras in ${\mathcal{V}}$}\left\}\,\,\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{\,\parbox{204.85974pt}{\rm Unitary pointed pivotal module tensor\;\! categories over ${\mathcal{V}}$, with chosen state}\,\right\}\right.\right.\!\!.

Moreover,
​​
when
{\mathcal{V}}
is ribbon,
spherical unitary anchored planar algebras correspond under this equivalence to unitary module tensor categories whose chosen state is spherical.

1.1
Motivations for this article

1.1.1
Enriched subfactor theory

The development of planar algebras
[
Jon21
]
is intimately linked to subfactor theory.
We expect a similar relation to hold between anchored planar algebras and
enriched
subfactor theory.
In their paper
[
JP17
]
, Corey Jones and the second author introduced a notion of
\rm W^{*}
-algebra object
A
internal to a unitary tensor category
{\mathcal{V}}
.
One could imagine formulating an analog of the notion of
\rm II_{1}
factor internal to
{\mathcal{V}}
(perhaps just the condition that the neutral part of
A
, i.e.
{\mathcal{V}}(1\to A)
, is a
\rm II_{1}
factor) and, similarly, a notion of subfactor internal to
{\mathcal{V}}
.

We conjecture that, in this context, the correct analog of the standard invariant is that of a unitary anchored planar algebra:

Conjecture 1.1
.

The enriched standard invariant of a subfactor internal to
{\mathcal{V}}
is a 2-shaded unitary anchored planar algebra in
Z({\mathcal{V}})
.
Finite index, finite depth hyperfinite
\rm II_{1}
subfactors internal to
{\mathcal{V}}
are classified by their enriched standard invariants
4
4

4

The relevant anchored planar algebras should satisfy
{\mathcal{P}}[0]=I(1)
, where
I:{\mathcal{V}}\to Z({\mathcal{V}})
is the adjoint of the forgetful functor
{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathcal{V}})\to{\mathcal{V}}
.
.

As an example, in
[
JL17
, Rem. 6.1]
,
Jaffe and Liu construct a subfactor from the inductive limit of parafermion algebras, and obtain the parafermion
subfactor planar para algebra
from its ‘graded standard invariant.’
Planar para algebras are anchored planar algebras internal to
{\mathcal{V}}=\mathsf{Vect}({\mathbb{Z}}/N)
with a particular braiding (see
[
HPT23b
, Examples 3.7 and 3.8]
), and the parafermion planar para algebra corresponds to a Tambara-Yamagami module tensor category over
{\mathcal{V}}
.

There is a classification of
\rm II_{1}
subfactors with index less than 4
[
Jon83
,
GdlHJ89
,
Kaw95
,
BN91
,
Izu94
]
in terms of ADE Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams (where
D_{\text{odd}}
and
E_{7}
do not occur, and
E_{6}
and
E_{8}
occur twice).
For subfactors enriched over super vector spaces, the non-simply laced Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams
C_{\text{even}}
and
F_{4}
also appear
[
ALW19
, §6-7]
.

1.1.2
Internal structure of bicommutant categories

Bicommutant categories were introduced in
[
Hen17b
]
, as higher categorical analogs of von Neumann algebras.
The simplest example of a bicommutant category is
{\sf Bim}(M)
, the tensor category of all bimodules over a von Neumann algebra
M
.
Examples corresponding to unitary fusion categories were constructed in
[
HP17
]
, and further studied in
[
HP23
]
.
Examples corresponding to conformal nets were constructed in
[
Hen17a
]
.

When
M=R
is a hyperfinite
\rm II_{1}
,
\rm II_{\infty}
, or
\rm III_{1}
factor,
there is a well-known correspondence
[
Pop90
,
Pop95
,
Jon21
,
Tom21
,
BCE+20
]
between conjugacy classes of finite depth
R
-
R
bimodules and isomorphism classes of unitary finite depth planar algebras
5
5

5

Unoriented planar algebras correspond to symmetrically self-dual bimodules.
Arbitrary finite depth bimodules are classified by planar algebras whose strands are oriented.
:

\left\{\parbox{145.10922pt}{Finite depth $R$-$R$-bimodules
}\!\left\}\left/\text{conj.}\,\leftrightarrow\,\,\,\left\{\parbox{128.0374pt}{Connected finite depth \centerline{\hbox{unitary planar algebras}}
}\right\}\right.\right.\right.\!\!\bigg/\text{iso.}

We conjecture that, under suitable assumptions, conjugacy clases of finite depth objects in a bicommutant category
{\mathcal{T}}
are in bijective correspondence with finite depth unitary anchored planar algebras in
Z({\mathcal{T}})
.

Conjecture 1.2
.

Let
{\mathcal{T}}
be a bicommutant category whose Drinfeld center
Z({\mathcal{T}})
is fusion. Then, under suitable assumptions, there exists a natural bijective correspondence

\left\{\parbox{130.88284pt}{\rm Finite depth objects of ${\mathcal{T}}$
}\!\left\}\left/\text{\rm conj.}\,\leftrightarrow\,\,\,\left\{\parbox{176.407pt}{\rm Connected finite depth unitary \centerline{\hbox{\rm anchored planar algebras in ${\mathcal{Z}}({\mathcal{T}})$}}
}\right\}\right.\right.\right.\!\!\bigg/\text{\rm iso.}

For bicommutant categories coming from fusion categories, Conjecture
1.2
was proven in our recent paper
[
HPT23a
]
.

1.1.3
(2+1)D topological orders

Topological order is a phenomenon in (theoretical) condensed matter physics beyond Landau’s symmetry breaking paradigm.
In
(2
+
1)
dimensions, the low energy effective field theory of a topologically ordered phase of matter is a topological quantum field theory, and the low energy localised excitations form a unitary modular tensor category (UMTC).

Conjecture 1.3
.

Let
{\mathcal{X}}
and
{\mathcal{Y}}
be
(2+1)
D topological orders with the same anomaly, let
{\mathcal{M}}
be a topological domain wall between them, and let
m
be a symmetrically self-dual point-like excitation that lives on
{\mathcal{M}}
.
Then the collection of objects

Material
{\mathcal{X}}
Material
{\mathcal{Y}}

(where the red dots represent
m
)
in the unitary modular tensor category associated to
{\mathcal{X}}
are the box-spaces of a unitary anchored planar algebra.

More generally, if
{\mathcal{U}}
is any unitary 3-category (a notion yet to be defined) and
c:v\to w
is a dualizable 1-morphism between dualizable objects,
then
{\mathcal{V}}:=\End(1_{v})
should be a unitary modular ribbon category and
{\mathcal{C}}:=\End(c)
should be a unitary
{\mathcal{V}}
-module multifusion category.
Moreover, for
m:c\Rightarrow c
symmetrically self-dual, the objects
\underline{\Hom}(1_{c},m^{\otimes k})\in{\mathcal{V}}
should form the box-spaces of a unitary anchored planar algebra.

Indeed, it should be the case that (2+1)D topological orders with the a given anomaly form a unitary 3-category whose 1-morphisms are topological domain walls and whose higher morphisms correspond to topological defects of higher codimension.
More precisely,
[
HBJP23
]
posits that for a UMTC
{\mathcal{A}}
whose Witt class represents an anomaly, the 3-category of
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched unitary fusion categories describes this putative 3-category of (2+1)D topological orders.

1.1.4
Unitary higher categories

Over the past decades, a theory of higher linear algebra has
emerged from work of many authors, e.g.,
[
BD95
,
Bae97
,
Lur09
,
HV19
]
.
The higher
n
-category
n\mathsf{Vect}
of
n
-
vector spaces
may be used as target for
n
-dimensional topological quantum field
theories, where the fully dualizable objects give fully extended
theories by the corbordism hypothesis.
Until recently, definitions of

n\mathsf{Vect}
were bespoke, chosen to agree with well-known state-sum models.
The recent breakthrough
[
GJF19
]
provides a uniform framework to
construct (the fully dualizable part of)
n\mathsf{Vect}
via a formal inductive procedure starting from just the complex numbers.

Starting with
{\mathbb{C}}
, a commutative algebra,
we can deloop and complete to obtain the 1-category
\mathsf{Vect_{fd}}
.
Since
\mathsf{Vect}
is a symmetric monoidal tensor category,
we can deloop and complete again to obtain the 2-category
\mathsf{Alg_{fd}^{sep}}
of finite dimensional separable algebras, bimodules, and intertwiners.
Assigning to an algebra its category of modules gives an equivalence to
2\mathsf{Vect}
, the 2-category of finite semisimple categories, linear functors, and natural transformations.
Since
2\mathsf{Vect}
is a symmetric monoidal 2-category, we may deloop and complete again to obtain the 3-category of (separable) multifusion categories
[
JF22
]
, which is equivalent to the 3-category of semisimple 2-categories
[
DR18
,
Déc22
]
.

{\mathbb{C}}\xrightarrow{\Sigma}\mathsf{Vect_{fd}}\xrightarrow{\Sigma}\mathsf{Alg_{fd}^{sep}}\simeq\mathsf{LinCat_{fin}^{ss}}\xrightarrow[\text{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{MR4444089}{}{}]}}]{\Sigma}\mathsf{MultFusCat}\underset{\text{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{MR4372801}{}{}]}}}{\simeq}\mathsf{Lin2Cat_{fin}^{ss}}\xrightarrow{\Sigma}\cdots

(1)

For physical applications in topologically ordered phases of matter, it is important to have a version of the above construction that incorporates unitary structures at all levels.
However, extending this construction to the unitary setting is quite delicate.
Whereas dualizability is a
property
in the non-unitary setting, it is additional
structure
in the unitary setting
[
Yam04
,
Pen20
]
.
Thus
n{\sf Hilb}
should come with canonical involutions corresponding to duals at various levels.

Writing this article has allowed us to clarify these notions for
2{\sf Hilb}
. Here, a
2-Hilbert space

[
Bae97
]
is a linear category (enriched in finite dimensional vector spaces) equipped with Hilbert space structures on hom spaces satisfying

\langle f,h\circ g^{\dagger}\rangle_{b\to c}=\langle f\circ g,h\rangle_{a\to c}=\langle g,f^{\dagger}\circ h\rangle_{a\to b}\qquad\qquad\forall\,g:a\to b,\,f:b\to c,\,h:a\to c.

As pointed out in
[
GMP+23
, Rem. 3.6.1]
, 2-Hilbert spaces are the natural setting for defining the unitary Yoneda embedding
[
JP20
]
.
In turn, we have a well-behaved notion of
unitary adjunction
for dagger functors, which we describe in §
2.1
below.
In Proposition
2.8
(see also Remark
2.9
) we prove that unitary adjunction gives a canonical unitary dual functor on
2{\sf Hilb}
.
We expect this to be a key ingredient in defining higher dagger idempotents, for the unitary analog of (
1
).

1.2
Outline

In §
2
, we provide the preliminary background for this article, together with some new contributions for unitary and involutive categories.
We discuss the unitary Yoneda embedding and unitary adjunction in §
2.1
,
and we review unitary dual functors and spherical states in §
2.2
.
In §
2.3
,
we use the graphical calculus for the 2-category
\mathsf{Cat}
to transport involutive structures through adjunctions.

In §
3
, we review the notion of pivotal module tensor category over a braided pivotal category before introducing the unitary counterpart in §
3.2
.
We briefly review the graphical calculus of strings on tubes for the categorified trace from
[
HPT16
]
, and we study the adjoint of the unit map in §
3.3
.
In the spherical setting, we prove unitarity of the traciator in §
3.4
.

In §
4
, we review the notions of planar algebra and anchored planar algebra before introducing the unitary counterparts in §
4.3
.
We show that for a spherical unitary anchored planar algebra, the adjoint is compatible with the inside-out reflection of tangles in Proposition
4.8
.
Finally, in §
5
, we prove our main Theorem
A
.

Preliminaries

Our standard references for (unitary) tensor categories include
[
LR97
,
GLR85
,
Sel11
,
EGNO15
,
HPT16
,
Pen20
]
.

Let
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathbb{C}}
be the 2-category of
{\mathbb{C}}
-linear categories, linear
and
anti-linear functors, and natural transformations.
We only allow natural transformations between functors if they are either both linear or both anti-linear.
In this section, we shall often use the graphical calculus for
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathbb{C}}
, denoting linear categories by two-dimensional regions, functors by strands, and natural transformations by junctures.
As in
[
CP22
]
, we may identify a category
{\mathcal{A}}
with the category of
{\mathbb{C}}
-linear functors
\mathsf{Vect}\to{\mathcal{A}}
.
Given a functor
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
and objects
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
and
b\in{\mathcal{B}}
,
this allows us to give a graphical representation e.g. for a morphism
f:F(a)\to b
, as follows:

,

f:F(a)\to b
and

are called
mates
if they are mapped to one another under the natural isomorphism

\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}\big(F(a)\to b\big)

\displaystyle\,\,\cong\,\,{\mathcal{A}}\big(a\to G(b)\big)

\displaystyle f\qquad

\displaystyle\,\,\leftrightarrow\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\mate(f)

\displaystyle\mate(g)\,\,\,\,

\displaystyle\,\,\leftrightarrow\,\,\qquad g.

where the cup and cap represent the
unit and counit of the adjunction.

The operations of taking the mate are natural with respect to pre-composition and post-composition by another morphism:

(M1)

\mate(f_{2}\circ f_{1})=G(f_{2})\circ\mate(f_{1})

for all

f_{1}:F(a)\to b_{1}
and
f_{2}:b_{1}\to b_{2}
.

(M2)

\mate(g_{2}\circ g_{1})=\mate(g_{2})\circ F(g_{1})

for all

g_{1}:a_{1}\to a_{2}
and
g_{2}:a_{2}\to G(b)
.

2.1
The unitary Yoneda lemma and unitary adjunctions

In this section, we work with semisimple
\rm C^{*}
categories. (Note that every Cauchy complete
\rm C^{*}
category with finite dimensional hom spaces is semisimple
[
GMP+23
, §3.1.1]
.)

Definition 2.1
.

A unitary trace on a semisimple
\rm C^{*}
category
{\mathcal{A}}
is a collection of linear maps
\Tr_{a}:{\mathcal{A}}(a\to a)\to{\mathbb{C}}
, for all
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
, satisfying

•

\Tr_{a}(f\circ g)=\Tr_{b}(g\circ f)
for all
f:a\to b
and
g:b\to a
, and

•

The sesquilinear forms
\langle f,g\rangle_{a\to b}:=\Tr_{a}(g^{\dagger}\circ f)
are positive definite.

The above inner products satisfy

\langle f,h\circ g^{\dagger}\rangle_{b\to c}=\langle f\circ g,h\rangle_{a\to c}=\langle g,f^{\dagger}\circ h\rangle_{a\to b}\qquad\quad\forall\,g:a\to b,\,f:b\to c,\,h:a\to c,

(2)

equivalently

(-\circ g)^{\dagger}=-\circ g^{\dagger}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(f\circ-)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\circ-,

(3)

and thus equip
{\mathcal{A}}
with the structure of a
2-Hilbert space
in the sense of
[
Bae97
]
.
Conversely, one may recover the trace from the 2-Hilbert space structure by the formula
\Tr_{a}(f):=\langle f,\id_{a}\rangle_{a\to a}
.
The notion of semisimple
\rm C^{*}
category equipped with a unitary trace is thus equivalent to the notion of
2
-Hilbert space.

The first condition in (
3
) implies that for all
c\in{\mathcal{A}}
, the functor
{\mathcal{A}}(-\to c):{\mathcal{A}}^{\op}\to{\sf Hilb}
is a
\dagger
-functor, and the second equality implies that the
unitary Yoneda embedding

{\mathcal{A}}\,\,\,\hookrightarrow\,\,\,{\sf Fun}^{\dagger}({\mathcal{A}}^{\op}\to{\sf Hilb})

(4)

is a
\dagger
-functor (where
{\sf Fun}^{\dagger}({\mathcal{A}}^{\op}\to{\sf Hilb})
denotes the
\dagger
-category of
\dagger
-functors
{\mathcal{A}}^{\op}\to{\sf Hilb}
).

The above facts were first observed in
[
GMP+23
, Rem. 3.61 and footnote]
, and
we shall refer to them collectively as the
unitary Yoneda lemma
.
Note that the essential image of (
4
) is the same as its unitary essential image (using polar decomposition in
{\sf Fun}^{\dagger}({\mathcal{A}}^{\op}\to{\sf Hilb})
), so a
\dagger
-functor
{\mathcal{A}}^{\op}\to{\sf Hilb}
is unitarily representable if and only if the underlying functor is representable.
Given a
\dagger
-functor
F\in{\sf Fun}^{\dagger}({\mathcal{A}}^{\rm op}\to{\sf Hilb})
in the essential image of (
4
), a representing object is given by

c:=\bigoplus_{a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})}d_{a}^{-1}F(a)\otimes a,

(5)

where
d_{a}:=\Tr^{\mathcal{A}}_{a}(\id_{a})
,
\Irr({\mathcal{A}})
is a basis
6
6

6

A
basis
of a semisimple linear category is a collection of representatives of each isomorphism class of simple objects.
of
{\mathcal{A}}
, and we use the notation
\lambda H
to denote the Hilbert space with the same underlying vector space as
H
and inner product
\lambda\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle_{H}
. The rescaling of the inner product of
F(a)
ensures the unitarity of the isomorphism
{\mathcal{A}}(-\to c)\cong F
given by

{\mathcal{A}}\left(b\to\bigoplus_{a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})}d_{a}^{-1}F(a)\otimes a\right)\cong d_{b}^{-1}F(b)\otimes{\mathcal{A}}(b\to b)\xrightarrow{\id_{F(b)}\otimes(\id_{b}\mapsto 1)}F(b)

(6)

for
b\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})
.

Remark 2.2
.

If
{\mathcal{A}}
is finitely semisimple and
{\sf Hilb}
is taken to mean finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, then (
4
) is a
{\dagger}
-equivalence.

Definition 2.3
.

Let
({\mathcal{A}},\Tr^{\mathcal{A}})
and
({\mathcal{B}},\Tr^{\mathcal{B}})
be semisimple
\rm C^{*}
categories equipped with unitary traces.
A
unitary adjunction
, denoted
F\dashv^{\dagger}G
, consists of linear
\dagger
-functors
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
and
G:{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{A}}
and a family of unitary and natural isomorphisms

\psi_{a,b}:{\mathcal{B}}(F(a)\to b)\xrightarrow{\,\,\cong\,\,}{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b)).

(7)

If
F
and
G
are instead antilinear
\dagger
-functors, and
(
7
) is antiunitary, then adjunction
is called an
antiunitary adjunction
.

Remark 2.4
.

In the above definition, if we had merely required
F
and
G
to be (anti)linear functors, they would nevertheless automatically be
\dagger
-functors.
We prove that
G
is a dagger functor (the argument for
F
is similar).
For any
f\in{\mathcal{B}}(b_{1}\to b_{2})
, the following diagram commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b_{1}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}(F(a)\to b_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}(F(a)\to b_{2}).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{a,b_{1}}^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(f)\circ-}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f\circ-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{a,b_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}

Applying
\dagger
to all the arrows, by (
3
),
the following diagram also commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b_{1}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}(F(a)\to b_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}(F(a)\to b_{2}).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(f)^{\dagger}\circ-}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{a,b_{2}}^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{a,b_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f^{\dagger}\circ-)}

As
G(f^{\dagger})\circ-
also makes that second diagram commute,

G(f^{\dagger})\circ-=G(f)^{\dagger}\circ-
,
and hence
G(f^{\dagger})=G(f)^{\dagger}
.

Similarly,
whenever
F\dashv G
are adjoint functors between linear categories,
if (
7
) is (anti)linear,
then
F
and
G
are automatically (anti)linear functors.

The above facts are reminiscent of the well-known fact that if
H,K
are Hilbert spaces and
S:H\to K
and
T:K\to H
are two functions such that
\langle S\eta,\xi\rangle=\langle\eta,T\xi\rangle
for all
\eta\in H
and
\xi\in K
, then
S
and
T
are automatically bounded linear maps.

Lemma 2.5
.

Let
({\mathcal{A}},\Tr^{\mathcal{A}})
and
({\mathcal{B}},\Tr^{\mathcal{B}})
be semisimple
\rm C^{*}
categories with unitary traces, and let
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
be a linear
\dagger
-functor that has a right adjoint. Then
F
also has a unitary right adjoint.
The unitary right adjoint
G
is unique up to unique unitary natural isomorphism,
and given by

G(b)\,=\bigoplus_{a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})}d_{a}^{-1}{\mathcal{B}}\big(F(a)\to b\big)\otimes a.

(8)

The same holds true for antilinear
\dagger
-functors.

Proof.

The unitary right adjoint
G
, if it exists, sends
b\in{\mathcal{B}}
to the object representing the
\dagger
-functor

a\mapsto{\mathcal{B}}\big(F(a)\to b\big).

(9)

By the unitary Yoneda Lemma, such a representing object, if it exists, is unique up to unique unitary isomorphism.
We get (
8
) by
substituting (
9
) into
(
5
).
If
F
admits a right adjoint, the functors (
9
) are representable, hence unitarily representable, hence
F
admits a unitary right adjoint.

Finally, antilinear
\dagger
-functors are the same thing as linear
\dagger
-functors
{\mathcal{A}}\to\overline{{\mathcal{B}}}
, so the same results hold true for antilinear
\dagger
-functors.
∎

Lemma 2.6
.

If
\coev
and
\ev
are the unit and counit of an (anti-)unitary adjunction
F\dashv^{\dagger}G
, then
\ev^{\dagger}
and
\coev^{\dagger}
are the unit and counit of an (anti-)unitary adjunction
G\dashv^{\dagger}F
.

Proof.

The adjunction is given by

{\mathcal{A}}(G(b)\to a)\underset{\text{anti-unitary}}{\cong}{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b))\underset{\text{(anti-)unitary}}{\cong}{\mathcal{A}}(F(a)\to b)\underset{\text{anti-unitary}}{\cong}{\mathcal{A}}(b\to F(a)).

(10)

The first equivalence is anti-unitary as

\langle f,g\rangle_{G(b)\to a}=\Tr^{\mathcal{A}}(g^{\dagger}\circ f)=\Tr^{\mathcal{A}}(f\circ g^{\dagger})=\langle g^{\dagger},f^{\dagger}\rangle_{a\to G(b)},

and similarly for the third one.

If we set
a=G(b)
, the image of
\id_{G(b)}
under (
10
) is
\ev^{\dagger}
. So
\ev^{\dagger}
is the counit of the adjunction (
10
). Similarly, setting
b=F(a)
, we see that
\coev^{\dagger}
is the unit of the adjunction.
∎

Anticipating the notion of unitary dual functor (see §
2.2
below), we have the following result:

Proposition 2.8
.

Let
({\mathcal{A}},\Tr^{\mathcal{A}})
be a semisimple
\rm C^{*}
category equipped with a unitary trace, and let
\End^{\dagger}_{d}({\mathcal{A}})
be its category of dualizable linear dagger endofunctors.
Then the operation which sends a dagger functor
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{A}}
to its unitary adjoint defines a unitary dual functor on
\End^{\dagger}_{d}({\mathcal{A}})
.

The same holds true for the category of linear or antilinear
\dagger
-functors from
{\mathcal{A}}
to itself.

Proof.

Given a dualizable
\dagger
-functor
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{A}}
, we
write
F^{*}
for its unitary adjoint (which is unique up to unique unitary isomorphism).
We must show that
the canonical isomorphism
F^{*}G^{*}\Rightarrow(GF)^{*}
is unitary, and that for all
\theta:F\Rightarrow G
we have

is therefore unitary.

\displaystyle=\Tr^{\mathcal{A}}_{G^{*}(a)}(\theta_{a}^{*{\dagger}}\circ g^{\dagger}\circ f)

\displaystyle=\Tr^{\mathcal{A}}_{F^{*}(a)}(g^{\dagger}\circ f\circ\theta_{a}^{*{\dagger}})

\displaystyle=\langle f\circ\theta_{a}^{*{\dagger}},g\rangle,

where the second and fifth equalities hold by Lemmas
2.6
and
2.7
.
By the non-degeneracy of the pairing, we conclude that
\theta_{a}^{{\dagger}*}=\theta_{a}^{*{\dagger}}
.
∎

Remark 2.9
.

More generally, unitary adjoints provide a canonical unitary dual functor on the
\rm C^{*}
2-category of semisimple
\rm C^{*}
categories, dualizable dagger functors, and bounded natural transformations.

2.2
Unitary dual functors and spherical states

Let
{\mathcal{C}}
be a unitary multitensor category (aka semisimple rigid tensor C* category).
We recall the following definition from
[
Pen20
]
:

Definition 2.10
.

A
unitary dual functor
on
{\mathcal{C}}
is a choice of dual
(c^{\vee},\ev_{c},\coev_{c})
for each object
c\in{\mathcal{C}}
(where
\ev_{c}:c^{\vee}\otimes c\to 1
, and
\coev_{c}:1\to c\otimes c^{\vee}
satisfy the zigzag identities), such that the corresponding functor
\vee:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{C}}^{\rm mop}
is a dagger tensor functor:

f^{\vee{\dagger}}=f^{{\dagger}\vee}
, and
\nu_{a,b}:a^{\vee}\otimes b^{\vee}\to(b\otimes a)^{\vee}
is unitary.

Remark 2.11
.

Unlike dual functors, unitary dual functors are not unique – see
[
Pen20
]
.

By
[
Sel11
, Lem. 7.5]
,
[
Pen20
, Cor. 3.10]
,
a unitary dual functor induces a pivotal structrue on
{\mathcal{C}}
by

\varphi_{c}:=(1\otimes\ev_{c})\circ(\ev_{c^{\vee}}^{\dagger}\otimes 1)=(\coev_{c}^{\dagger}\otimes 1)\circ(1\otimes\coev_{c^{\vee}}):c\to c^{\vee\vee},

(11)

and
\varphi_{c}
is unitary for all
c\in{\mathcal{C}}
.

A unitary dual functor
\vee
on a unitary multitensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
gives two
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
-valued traces
\tr_{L}
and
\tr_{R}
on the underlying
\rm C^{*}
category.

Definition 2.12
.

A
spherical state
on a unitary multitensor category with unitary dual functor
({\mathcal{C}},\vee)
is a state
\psi
on
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
such that
\psi\circ\tr_{L}(f)=\psi\circ\tr_{R}(f)
for every
f\in\End_{\mathcal{C}}(c)
.
Given a spherical state
\psi
, we write
\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}:=\psi\circ\tr_{L}
.

Lemma 2.13
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{C}}
is an indecomposable unitary multitensor category.

(1)

A unitary dual functor admits at most one spherical state.

(2)

For each state
\psi
on
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
, there is a unique unitary dual functor with respect to which
\psi
is spherical.

We thus have a bijection

\left\{\parbox{156.49014pt}{\rm\centerline{\hbox{Unitary dual functors $\vee$ which}}\centerline{\hbox{admit a spherical state $\psi$}}}\right\}\cong\left\{\parbox{68.28644pt}{\rm\centerline{\hbox{States $\psi$}}\centerline{\hbox{on $\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})$}}}\right\}.

Proof.

Let
{\mathcal{U}}
be the universal grading groupoid of
{\mathcal{C}}
.
By
[
Pen20
, Thm. A]
, unitary dual functors
\vee
on
{\mathcal{C}}
are classified by
groupoid homomorphisms
\pi:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}
,
where
\vee
corresponds to
\pi
if

\exists\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}},\,\,\,\,\coev_{c}^{\dagger}\circ(f\otimes\id_{c^{\vee_{\pi}}})\circ\coev_{c}=\lambda p_{i},\qquad\ev_{c}\circ(\id_{c^{\vee_{\pi}}}\otimes f)\circ\ev_{c}^{\dagger}=\pi_{\operatorname{gr}(c)}\cdot\lambda p_{j}

(12)

for all homogeneous
c\in 1_{i}\otimes{\mathcal{C}}\otimes 1_{j}
(homogeneous w.r.t. the
{\mathcal{U}}
-grading) and
f:c\to c
.
Here,
p_{1},\ldots,p_{r}\in\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
are the projections onto the simple summands of
1_{\mathcal{C}}
, and
\operatorname{gr}_{c}\in{\mathcal{U}}
is the
{\mathcal{U}}
-grading of
c
.

If
\vee
admits a spherical state
\psi
, then
\pi
factors through the ‘matrix groupoid’
{\mathcal{M}}_{r}
with
r
objects and a unique isomorphism between any two objects.
Indeed, applying the spherical state
\psi
to (
12
), we have

\lambda\psi(p_{i})=\pi_{\operatorname{gr}(c)}\lambda\psi(p_{j})
,
and thus

\pi_{\operatorname{gr}(c)}=\psi(p_{i})/\psi(p_{j})=:\pi_{ij}

(13)

Since
\sum_{i}\psi(p_{i})=1
, (
13
) completely determines
\psi
in terms of
\pi
.
This proves part (1) of the lemma.
Equation (
13
) also determines
\pi
in terms of
\psi
, so there is at most one unitary dual functor
\vee
for which a given state
\psi
can be spherical.
It remains to verify that
\psi
is spherical for the unitary dual functor associated to the homomrphism
\pi
defined in (
13
):

\psi(\tr_{L}(f))=\lambda\pi_{ij}\psi(p_{j})=\lambda\frac{\psi(p_{i})}{\psi(p_{j})}\psi(p_{j})=\lambda\psi(p_{i})=\psi(\tr_{R}(f)).

This proves part (2) of the lemma.
∎

Observe that (2) of Lemma
2.13
holds even when
{\mathcal{C}}
is decomposable.
Indeed, we can just restrict (and rescale)
\psi
to each indecomposable summand and then apply the lemma.

Definition 2.14
.

A unitary multitensor category with unitary dual functor
({\mathcal{C}},\vee)
is called
spherical
if it admits a spherical state.

Warning 2.15
.

There exists an alternative possible definition of sphericality
for a unitary multitensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
, that we will not be using in this article:
the unitary dual functor corresponding to
\pi=1
in (
12
).
This is the
balanced
, or
minimal
unitary dual functor studied in
[
BDH14
]
.

Definition 2.16
.

Suppose
({\mathcal{C}},\varphi^{\mathcal{C}})
and
({\mathcal{D}},\varphi^{\mathcal{D}})
are pivotal categories.
A monoidal functor
F:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
is called
pivotal
if the canonical isomorphism

\chi_{c}:=\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to101.65pt{\vbox to43.08pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 42.28639pt\lower-28.65276pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

\lxSVG@closescope }}}

(where we have suppressed the tensorator of
F
)
satisfies
(\chi_{c})^{\vee}\circ\varphi^{\mathcal{D}}_{F(c)}=\chi_{c^{\vee}}\circ F(\varphi^{\mathcal{C}}_{c})
.

By
[
Pen20
, Prop. 3.40]
, when
{\mathcal{C}}
and
{\mathcal{D}}
are unitary multitensor categories equipped with unitary dual functors, pivotality of
F
is equivalent to the canonical isomorphisms
\chi_{c}

being unitary.

Recall that a unitary tensor category is a unitary multitensor category with simple unit.

Lemma 2.17
.

Let

({\mathcal{C}},\vee_{\mathcal{C}})
and
({\mathcal{D}},\vee_{\mathcal{D}})
be unitary multitensor categories equipped with unitary dual functors, with
1_{\mathcal{C}}
simple (i.e.
{\mathcal{C}}
is a tensor category), and
{\mathcal{D}}
non-zero.
If
{\mathcal{D}}
is spherical and
F:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
is a pivotal dagger tensor functor, then
{\mathcal{C}}
is spherical.

Proof.

Let
c\in{\mathcal{C}}
be any object.
By the pivotality of
F
and
[
Pen20
, Lem. 2.14]
,

F(\tr_{L}^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c}))=\tr^{\mathcal{D}}_{L}(\id_{F(c)})\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(\tr_{R}^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c}))=\tr^{\mathcal{D}}_{R}(\id_{F(c)}).

(14)

Since
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
is one-dimensional,
\tr_{L}^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c})
and
\tr_{R}^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c})
are scalars. So the two quantities in (
14
) are scalar multiples of
\id_{1_{\mathcal{D}}}
.
Let
\psi
be the spherical state of
{\mathcal{D}}
.
The above two scalars are unchanged under applying
\psi
, so

\tr^{\mathcal{D}}_{L}(\id_{F(c)})=(\psi\circ\tr^{\mathcal{D}}_{L})(\id_{F(c)})=(\psi\circ\tr^{\mathcal{D}}_{R})(\id_{F(c)})=\tr^{\mathcal{D}}_{R}(\id_{F(c)}).

It follows that
\tr_{L}^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c})=\tr_{R}^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c})
.
∎

We end this section by explaining how a unitary dual functor on a unitary multitensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
induces a unitary dual functor on its unitary Drinfeld center
Z^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
(the full subcategory of the ordinary Drinfeld center
Z({\mathcal{C}})
where all half-braidings are unitary):

Lemma 2.18
.

Let
\vee=(\vee,\ev,\coev)
be a unitary dual functor on
{\mathcal{C}}
.
Then
\vee
canonically induces a unitary dual functor on
Z^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
.

Proof.

Given an object
(X,\sigma_{X})\in Z^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
, we define
(X,\sigma_{X})^{\vee}:=(X^{\vee},\sigma_{X^{\vee}})
where

\sigma_{X^{\vee},Y}:=(\ev_{X}\otimes\id_{Y}\otimes\id_{X^{\vee}})\circ(\id_{X^{\vee}}\otimes\sigma_{X,Y}^{-1}\otimes\id_{X^{\vee}})\circ(\id_{X^{\vee}}\otimes\id_{Y}\otimes\coev_{X}).

The half-braiding
\sigma_{X^{\vee},Y}
is unitary.
The evaluation and coevaluation are morphisms in
{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathcal{C}})
hence in
{\mathcal{Z}}^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
.
Finally, since the (co)evaluations for
(X,\sigma_{X})
are the same as those of the underlying object
X
, the dual functor
(X,\sigma_{X})^{\vee}:=(X^{\vee},\sigma_{X^{\vee}})
is unitary.
∎

2.3
Involutive functors

An
involutive structure
on a category
{\mathcal{A}}
is an anti-linear functor
\overline{\,\cdot\,}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{A}}
together with a coherence natural isomorphism
\varphi:\id_{\mathcal{A}}\Rightarrow\overline{\overline{\,\cdot\,}}
satisfying
\overline{\varphi_{a}}=\varphi_{\overline{a}}
for all
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
.
In the graphical calculus for
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathbb{C}}
, we denote the anti-linear functor
\overline{\,\cdot\,}
by a thick red strand,
\varphi
by a cap, and
\varphi^{-1}
by a cup.

\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to17.07pt{\vbox to17.87pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.0pt\lower-0.4pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}

Definition 2.19
.

A
conjugate-linear
morphism from
a
to
b
, denoted
f:a\rightharpoonup b
, is a morphism
a\to\overline{b}
.

A
real structure
on an object
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
is the data of a conjugate-linear morphism
r:a\rightharpoonup a
such that
\overline{r}\circ r=\varphi_{a}
.

Definition 2.20
.

Let
{\mathcal{A}}
and
{\mathcal{B}}
be involutive categories.
An involutive functor
(F,\chi)
from
{\mathcal{A}}
to
{\mathcal{B}}
is a functor
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
equipped with a family of isomorphisms
\chi_{a}:F(\overline{a})\to\overline{F(a)}
, for
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
, satisfying

•

(involutive)

\overline{\chi_{a}}\circ\chi_{\overline{a}}\circ F(\varphi^{\mathcal{A}}_{a})=\varphi_{F(a)}^{\mathcal{B}}

•

(conjugate natural)

\overline{F(f)}\circ\chi_{a_{1}}=\chi_{a_{2}}\circ F(\overline{f})
for all
f:a_{1}\to a_{2}
.

A natural transformation
\theta
between two involutive functors
(F,\chi^{F}),(G,\chi^{G}):{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
is called
involutive
if
\chi^{G}_{a}\circ\theta_{\overline{a}}=\overline{\theta_{a}}\circ\chi^{F}_{a}:F(\overline{a})\to\overline{G(a)}
for all
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
.

In the graphical calculus for
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathbb{C}}
, we denote
\chi^{F}
by a crossing:

Lemma 2.22
.

Let
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
be an involutive functor
between involutive categories,
and let
G:{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{A}}
be its right adjoint
(with involutive structure
\chi^{G}
as in Proposition
2.21
).
Then, for all
f\in{\mathcal{B}}(F(a)\to b)
, we have

\overline{\mate(f)}=\chi^{G}_{b}\circ\mate(\overline{f}\circ\chi^{F}_{a})\in{\mathcal{A}}\big(\overline{a}\to\overline{G(b)}\big).

Similarly, for all
g\in{\mathcal{A}}(a\to G(b))
, we have

\overline{\mate(g)}=\mate\big([\chi_{b}^{G}]^{-1}\circ\overline{g}\big)\circ[\chi_{a}^{F}]^{-1}\in{\mathcal{B}}\big(\overline{F(a)}\to\overline{b}\big).

Proof.

We only prove the first equality, as the other one is similar.

The result is an instance of the final statement in Proposition

A bi-involutive category is an involutive category which is also a dagger category such that
\overline{\,\cdot\,}
is a dagger functor and
\varphi
is unitary.
A bi-involutive functor
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
between bi-involutive categories is an involutive functor
(F,\chi)
such that
F
is a dagger functor and
\chi
is unitary.

Corollary 2.23
.

Let
F:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
be a dualizable functor between semisimple bi-involutive categories with unitary traces.
Then its unitary adjoint
G:=F^{*}
is also bi-involutive, maning
\chi^{G}
(as defined in Proposition
2.21
) is unitary.

Proof.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}:={\mathcal{A}}\oplus{\mathcal{B}}
, and identify
F,G
with functors

\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
F&0\end{pmatrix}\,,\,\begin{pmatrix}0&G\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\,:\,{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{C}}.

\overline{\,\cdot\,}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{A}}
and
\overline{\,\cdot\,}:{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{B}}
assemble to a functor

\begin{pmatrix}\overline{\,\cdot\,}&0\\
0&\overline{\,\cdot\,}\end{pmatrix}\,:\,{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{C}}

that equips
{\mathcal{C}}
with the structure of a bi-involutive category.

Working in the category of dualizable linear or antiliner
\dagger
-functors from
{\mathcal{C}}
to itself (for which unitary adjoint defines a unitary dual functor by Proposition
2.8
),

\chi^{G}
is the
2\pi
-rotation of
\chi^{F}
.
The result follows from the fact that
\chi^{F}
is unitary,
and that the
2\pi
-rotation of a unitary under a unitary dual functor is again unitary.
∎

2.4
Involutive lax monoidal functors

An involutive monoidal category
[
Egg11
]
is a monoidal category
{\mathcal{C}}
equipped with an involutive structure
(\overline{\,\cdot\,},\varphi)
, and coherence natural isomorphisms
\nu_{a,b}:\overline{a}\otimes\overline{b}\to\overline{b\otimes a}
and real structure
r:1\to\overline{1}
(equivalently,
r:1\rightharpoonup 1
) which satisfy

•

(associativity)
\nu_{a,c\otimes b}\circ(\id_{\overline{a}}\otimes\nu_{b,c})=\nu_{b\otimes a,c}\circ(\nu_{a,b}\otimes\id_{\overline{c}})

•

(unitality)
\nu_{1,a}\circ(r\otimes\id_{\overline{a}})=\id_{\overline{a}}=\nu_{a,1}\circ(\id_{\overline{a}}\otimes r)

•

(compatibility with
\varphi
)

\varphi_{a\otimes b}=\overline{\nu_{b,a}}\circ\nu_{\overline{a},\overline{b}}\circ(\varphi_{a}\otimes\varphi_{b})
.

By
[
Pen20
, §3.5]
,
a unitary multitensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
has a canonical involutive structure
\overline{\,\cdot\,}
. This involutive structure has the notable feature that for any choice of unitary dual functor
\vee
, the conjugate

\overline{x}
of an object
x
is canonically unitarily isomorphic to its unitary dual
x^{\vee}
.

Remark 2.24
.

Note that the tensor product of a conjugate-linear morphism with an ordinary morphism is meaningless. However, if
f:a\rightharpoonup b
and
g:a^{\prime}\rightharpoonup b^{\prime}
are two conjugate-linear morphisms, then we may define

f\otimes g:a\otimes a^{\prime}\rightharpoonup b^{\prime}\otimes b

as the composite

a\otimes a^{\prime}\xrightarrow{f\otimes g}\overline{b}\otimes\overline{b^{\prime}}\xrightarrow{\nu_{b,b^{\prime}}}\overline{b^{\prime}\otimes b}.

Recall that a monoidal functor
F:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
between monoidal categories involves coherences
\iota^{F}:1_{\mathcal{D}}\to F(1_{\mathcal{C}})
,
and
\mu_{a,b}^{F}:F(a)\otimes F(b)\to F(a\otimes b)
.

Definition 2.25
.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}
and
{\mathcal{D}}
be involutive monoidal categories.
An involutive (lax) monoidal functor
(F,\mu,\iota,\chi):{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
is an involutive functor
(F,\chi):{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
such that
(F,\mu,\iota):{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
is (lax) monoidal, and such that the following additional conditions hold:

•

(unitality)

\chi_{1_{\mathcal{C}}}\circ F(r_{\mathcal{C}})\circ\iota=\overline{\iota}\circ r_{{\mathcal{D}}}
.

•

(monoidality)

\chi_{d\otimes c}\circ F(\nu_{c,d})\circ\mu_{\overline{c},\overline{d}}=\overline{\mu_{d,c}}\circ\nu_{F(c),F(d)}\circ(\chi_{c}\otimes\chi_{d})

Recall that the right adjoint
G:{\mathcal{D}}\to{\mathcal{C}}
of a monoidal functor
(F,\mu^{F},\iota^{F}):{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
is lax monoidal by
[
Kel74
]
.
Indeed,
\mu^{G}_{d_{1},d_{2}}:G(d_{1})\otimes G(d_{2})\to G(d_{1}\otimes d_{2})
is the mate of

(\varepsilon_{d_{1}}\otimes\varepsilon_{d_{2}})\circ(\mu^{F}_{G(d_{1}),G(d_{2})})^{-1}

under the adjunction

{\mathcal{C}}\big(G(d_{1})\otimes G(d_{2})\to G(d_{1}\otimes d_{2})\big)\,\cong\,{\mathcal{D}}\big(F(G(d_{1})\otimes G(d_{2}))\to d_{1}\otimes d_{2}\big),

and
\iota^{G}:1_{\mathcal{C}}\to G(1_{\mathcal{D}})
is the mate of
(\iota^{F})^{-1}
under the adjunction

{\mathcal{C}}\big(1_{\mathcal{C}}\to G(1_{\mathcal{D}})\big)\,\cong\,{\mathcal{D}}\big(F(1_{\mathcal{C}})\to 1_{\mathcal{D}}\big).

Proposition 2.26
.

Let
(F,\mu^{F},\iota^{F},\chi^{F}):{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}
be an involutive monoidal functor between involutive monoidal categories.
Then its right adjoint
(G,\mu,\iota):{\mathcal{D}}\to{\mathcal{C}}
is involutive lax monoidal, with

\iota^{G}
and
\mu^{G}
as above, and

\chi^{G}
as in Proposition
2.21
.

Proof.

We need to check the two conditions in Definition
2.25
.
To prove unitality, we will argue that

\iota^{G}\circ r_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}=G(r_{\mathcal{D}}^{-1})\circ\chi_{1_{\mathcal{D}}}^{-1}\circ\overline{\iota^{G}}:\overline{1_{\mathcal{C}}}\to G(1_{\mathcal{D}})
.
Taking mates under the adjunction

{\mathcal{C}}\big(\overline{1_{\mathcal{C}}}\to G(1_{\mathcal{D}})\big)\,\cong\,{\mathcal{D}}\big(F(\overline{1_{\mathcal{C}}})\to 1_{\mathcal{D}}\big),

the resulting morphisms
fit in the following pasting diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{1_{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(1_{\mathcal{C}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FG(1_{\mathcal{D}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{G(1_{\mathcal{D}})})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{FG(1_{\mathcal{D}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{F(1_{\mathcal{C}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FG(\overline{1_{\mathcal{D}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{1_{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1_{\mathcal{D}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{\iota^{G}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(r_{\mathcal{C}}^{-1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{F}_{1_{\mathcal{C}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\iota^{G})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{1_{\mathcal{D}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F((\chi_{1_{\mathcal{D}}}^{G})^{-1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{F}_{G(1_{\mathcal{D}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\varepsilon_{1_{\mathcal{D}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{F(\iota^{G})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{\overline{1_{\mathcal{D}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\iota^{F}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{\mathcal{D}}^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota^{F}}

Going right and then down is the mate of

\iota^{G}\circ r_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}
,
and going down and then right is the mate of

G(r_{\mathcal{D}}^{-1})\circ\chi_{1_{\mathcal{D}}}^{-1}\circ\overline{\iota^{G}}
.
The triangles commute by the definition of
\iota^{G}
.
The bottom left quadrilateral commutes using the dfinition of
(\chi^{G})^{-1}
.
And the middle pentagon is the unitality condition for
F
in Definition
2.25
.

To prove monoidality, we argue that

G(\nu^{\mathcal{D}}_{d_{1},d_{2}})\circ\mu_{\overline{d_{1}},\overline{d_{2}}}\circ(\chi^{-1}_{d_{1}}\otimes\chi^{-1}_{d_{2}})=\chi_{d_{1}\otimes d_{2}}^{-1}\circ\overline{\mu_{d_{2},d_{1}}}\circ\nu^{\mathcal{C}}_{G(d_{1}),G(d_{2})}:\overline{G(d_{1})}\otimes\overline{G(d_{2})}\to G(\overline{d_{2}\otimes d_{1}})

Taking mates under the adjunction

{\mathcal{C}}\big(\overline{G(d_{1})}\otimes\overline{G(d_{2})}\to G(\overline{d_{2}\otimes d_{1}})\big)\,\cong\,{\mathcal{D}}\big(F(\overline{G(d_{1})}\otimes\overline{G(d_{2})})\to\overline{d_{2}\otimes d_{1}}\big),

the resulting maps fit in the following pasting diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{G(d_{1})}\otimes\overline{G(d_{2})})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(G(\overline{d_{1}})\otimes G(\overline{d_{2}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FG(\overline{d_{1}}\otimes\overline{d_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{G(d_{1})})\otimes F(\overline{G(d_{2})})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FG(\overline{d_{1}})\otimes FG(\overline{d_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{FG(d_{1})}\otimes\overline{FG(d_{2})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{d_{1}}\otimes\overline{d_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{G(d_{2})\otimes G(d_{1})})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{F(G(d_{2})\otimes G(d_{1}))}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{FG(d_{2})\otimes FG(d_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{G(d_{2}\otimes d_{1})})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{FG(d_{2}\otimes d_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(G(\overline{d_{1}\otimes d_{2}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{d_{2}\otimes d_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\nu_{G(d_{1}),G(d_{2})}^{\mathcal{C}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F((\chi^{G}_{d_{1}})^{-1}\otimes(\chi^{G}_{d_{2}})^{-1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\mu^{G}_{\overline{d_{1}},\overline{d_{2}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{\overline{d_{1}}\otimes\overline{d_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu^{F}_{\overline{G(d_{1})},\overline{G(d_{2})}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F((\chi^{G}_{d_{1}})^{-1})\otimes F((\chi^{G}_{d_{2}})^{-1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{F}_{G(d_{1})}\otimes\chi^{F}_{G(d_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu^{F}_{G(\overline{d_{1}}),G(\overline{d_{2}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{\overline{d_{1}}}\otimes\varepsilon_{\overline{d_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{\mathcal{D}}_{FG(d_{1}),FG(d_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\varepsilon_{d_{1}}}\otimes\overline{\varepsilon_{d_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{\mathcal{D}}_{d_{1},d_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{F}_{G(d_{2})\otimes G(d_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\overline{\mu^{G}_{d_{2},d_{1}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{F(\mu^{G}_{d_{2},d_{1}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\mu^{F}_{G(d_{2}),G(d_{1})}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\varepsilon_{d_{2}}\otimes\varepsilon_{d_{1}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{F}_{G(d_{2}\otimes d_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F((\chi^{G}_{d_{1}\otimes d_{2}})^{-1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\varepsilon_{d_{2}\otimes d_{1}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{\overline{d_{2}\otimes d_{1}}}}

Going right and then down is the mate of

G(\nu^{\mathcal{D}}_{d_{1},d_{2}})\circ\mu_{\overline{d_{1}},\overline{d_{2}}}\circ(\chi^{-1}_{d_{1}}\otimes\chi^{-1}_{d_{2}})
,
while going down and then right is the mate of

\chi_{d_{1}\otimes d_{2}}^{-1}\circ\overline{\mu_{d_{2},d_{1}}}\circ\nu^{\mathcal{C}}_{G(d_{1}),G(d_{2})}
.
The hexagon in the top left is the monoidality condition for
F
in Definition
2.25
.

3
Unitary module tensor categories

3.1
Module tensor categories

Let
{\mathcal{V}}
be a braided tensor category.
A module tensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
over
{\mathcal{V}}
is a tensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
equipped with an “action” of
{\mathcal{V}}
in the following sense:

Definition 3.1
.

A
module tensor category
over
{\mathcal{V}}
is a tensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
together with a braided tensor functor
\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}:{\mathcal{V}}\to{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathcal{C}})
from
{\mathcal{V}}
to the Drinfeld center of
{\mathcal{C}}
.
If
{\mathcal{V}}
and
{\mathcal{C}}
are pivotal and if
\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}
is a pivotal functor, then we call
{\mathcal{C}}
a pivotal module tensor category.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}
be a pivotal module tensor category over
{\mathcal{V}}
, and let us write
\varphi_{a}:a\to a^{\vee\vee}
for the pivotal structure of
{\mathcal{C}}
.
A
pointing
of
{\mathcal{C}}
is a choice of object
c\in{\mathcal{C}}
such that
c
and
\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}({\mathcal{V}})
generate
{\mathcal{C}}
under the operations of tensor product, direct sum, and taking direct summands.
We also require that our chosen object
c
comes equipped with a
symmetric self-duality
isomorphism
r_{c}:c\to c^{\vee}
satisfying
\ev_{c}\circ(r_{c}\otimes\id_{c})=\ev_{c^{\vee}}\circ(\varphi_{c}\otimes r_{c})
.
7
7

7

As explained in
[
HPT23b
, Section 3.2.1]
, this last requirement is not crucial.
We could deal with objects that are not self-dual at the cost of equipping all strands with co-orientations (and see
[
HP23
, Section 4.1]
for why co-orientations are preferable to orientations).

Construction 3.2
.

Let
({\mathcal{C}},\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}})
be a pivotal module tensor over
{\mathcal{V}}
.
Suppose that the functor
\Phi:=\Forget_{\mathcal{Z}}\circ\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}:{\mathcal{V}}\to{\mathcal{C}}
admits a right adjoint, denoted
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}
(where
\Forget_{\mathcal{Z}}:{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathcal{C}})\to{\mathcal{C}}
is the forgetful functor).
In
[
HPT16
]
, we showed that

\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{V}}

has a canonical structure of a
categorified trace
. It comes equipped with the following structure.

unit

\eta_{v}:v\to\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\Phi(v))

and

counit

\varepsilon_{x}:\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(x))\to x

of the adjunction.

Definition 3.3
.

A 1-morphism
({\mathcal{C}}_{1},\Phi_{1}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}},\varphi^{1},x_{1})\to({\mathcal{C}}_{2},\Phi_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}},\varphi^{2},x_{2})

of pivotal pointed module tensor categories is a pair
(G,\gamma)
consisting of:

•

a pivotal tensor functor
G:{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2}
such that
G(x_{1})=x_{2}
and
r_{2}=\chi_{x_{1}}\circ G(r_{1})
, where
r_{i}:x_{i}\to x_{i}^{\vee}
is the symmetric self-duality, and
\chi
is as in Definition
2.16
.

•

an
action coherence
monoidal natural isomorphism
\gamma:\Phi_{2}\Rightarrow G\circ\Phi_{1}
satisfying the following compatibility with the half-braidings:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi_{2}(v)\otimes G(c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(\Phi_{1}(v))\otimes G(c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(\Phi_{1}(v)\otimes c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(c)\otimes\Phi_{2}(v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(c)\otimes G(\Phi_{1}(v))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(c\otimes\Phi_{1}(v))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{v}\otimes\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{\Phi_{2}(v),G(c)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(e_{\Phi_{1}(v),c})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\otimes\gamma_{v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}

Given two 1-morphisms
(G,\gamma^{G}),(H,\gamma^{H})
between pointed module tensor categories, by
[
HPT23b
, Lem. 3.6]
, there is at most one monoidal natural transformation
\kappa:(G,\gamma^{G})\Rightarrow(H,\gamma^{H})
satisfying the following compatibility with the action coherence morphisms:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi_{2}(v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(\Phi_{1}(v))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(\Phi_{1}(v))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma^{G}_{v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma^{H}_{v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\kappa_{\Phi_{1}(v)}}

When such a
\kappa
exists, it is necessarily invertible.
Hence the 2-category of pointed pivotal module tensor categories over
{\mathcal{V}}
is 1-truncated, i.e., equivalent to a 1-category.

3.2
Unitary module tensor categories

For the remainder of this section, we assume that
({\mathcal{V}},\vee_{\mathcal{V}})
is a braided unitary tensor category with a fixed unitary dual functor,
and let
\tr^{\mathcal{V}}
be the associated right pivotal trace.

Definition 3.4
.

Let
{\mathcal{V}}
be as above.
A
unitary module (multi)tensor category
over
{\mathcal{V}}
is a unitary (multi)tensor category
{\mathcal{C}}
with a unitary dual functor
\vee_{\mathcal{C}}
, a faithful state
\psi_{\mathcal{C}}
on
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
, and
a braided pivotal dagger tensor functor
\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}:{\mathcal{V}}\to{\mathcal{Z}}^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
.

We call a unitary module multitensor category
spherical
if
\psi_{\mathcal{C}}
is a spherical state (Definition
2.12
).
See Warning
2.15
.
Observe that, by Lemma
2.17
,
the existence of a non-zero spherical unitary
{\mathcal{V}}
-module tensor category implies that
{\mathcal{V}}
is ribbon, i.e., that the unitary dual functor on
{\mathcal{V}}
is spherical.

The choices of
\vee_{\mathcal{C}}
and
\psi_{\mathcal{C}}
endow
{\mathcal{C}}
with a unitary trace

\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}:=\psi_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\tr^{\vee}_{R}.

(15)

Moreover,
({\mathcal{C}},\Tr^{\mathcal{C}})
is a pivotal module
\rm C^{*}
category (aka unitary module category)
[
GMP+23
, §3.6.2]
for the underlying unitary tensor category of
{\mathcal{V}}
(without the braiding).
So unitary module tensor categories are, in particular, unitary module categories.

Remark 3.5
.

Suppose
({\mathcal{C}},\vee_{\mathcal{C}},\psi_{\mathcal{C}},\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}})
is a unitary module multitensor category over
{\mathcal{V}}
.
If
\Phi
admits a right adjoint, then by Lemma
2.5
,
\Phi
admits a right unitary adjoint

\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}
which is automatically bi-involutive lax monoidal by
Proposition
2.26

and
Corollary
2.23
.
Thus
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}
comes equipped with canonical unitary isomorphisms
\{\chi^{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}}_{c}:\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{c})\to\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(c)}\}_{c\in{\mathcal{C}}}
satisfying the axioms in Definitions
2.20
and
2.25
.

We warn the reader that
\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}
is a trace in the sense of Definition
2.1
, whereas
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}
is a categorified trace as described in Construction
3.2
.

As before, a
pointing
of
{\mathcal{C}}
is a choice of object
c\in{\mathcal{C}}
such that
c
and
\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}({\mathcal{V}})
generate
{\mathcal{C}}
under the operations of tensor product, orthogonal direct sum, and taking orthogonal direct summands.
We also require that our symmetric self-duality
r_{c}:c\to c^{\vee}
is unitary; this is also called a
real structure
for
c
.

Definition 3.6
.

A 1-morphism
(G,\gamma):({\mathcal{C}}_{1},\vee_{1},\psi_{1},\Phi_{1}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}},x_{1})\to({\mathcal{C}}_{2},\vee_{2},\psi_{2},\Phi_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}},x_{2})

of pointed unitary module tensor categories over
{\mathcal{V}}
is a 1-morphism of underlying pointed pivotal module tensor categories such that

•

G
is a
{\dagger}
-tensor functor,

•

the action coherence monoidal natural isomorphism
\gamma:\Phi_{2}\Rightarrow G\circ\Phi_{1}
is unitary and involutive:

\forall v\in{\mathcal{V}},\,\overline{\gamma_{v}}\circ\chi^{\Phi_{2}}_{v}=\chi^{G}_{\Phi_{1}(v)}\circ G(\chi^{\Phi_{1}}_{v})\circ\gamma_{\overline{v}}:\Phi_{2}(\overline{v})\to\overline{G(\Phi_{1}(v))}
,

•

\psi_{2}\circ G=\psi_{1}
on
\End_{{\mathcal{C}}_{1}}(1_{{\mathcal{C}}_{1}})
.

4.3
below, we will define unitarity for an anchored planar algebra in terms of a certain pairing on

hence the right hand side is also equipped with the structure of an abelian
\rm C^{*}
-algebra.
The multiplication and
*
-structure on the right hand side of (
16
) are given by

x\cdot y=\mu_{1_{\mathcal{C}},1_{\mathcal{C}}}\circ(x\otimes y)\qquad\quad\text{and}\qquad\quad x^{*}=\big(\chi^{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}}_{1_{\mathcal{C}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(r_{\mathcal{C}})\big)^{-1}\circ\overline{x}\circ r_{\mathcal{V}}.

To see that the isomorphism (
16
) intertwines the two
*
-structures, i.e.,

\displaystyle\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(f^{\dagger})\circ i=(\chi_{1_{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(r_{{\mathcal{C}}}))^{-1}\circ\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(f)\circ i}\circ r_{{\mathcal{V}}},

equivalently

\displaystyle\chi_{1_{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(r_{{\mathcal{C}}})\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(f^{\dagger})\circ i=\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(f)\circ i}\circ r_{\mathcal{V}},

we check that, since
f^{\dagger}=\overline{f}^{\vee}=(r_{\mathcal{C}})^{-1}\circ\overline{f}\circ r_{\mathcal{C}}
on
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
(as
r_{\mathcal{C}}=\coev_{1}
), we have

\displaystyle\chi_{1_{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(r_{{\mathcal{C}}})\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(f^{\dagger})\circ i

\displaystyle=\chi_{1_{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}(r_{{\mathcal{C}}})\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(r_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1})\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{f})\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(r_{\mathcal{C}})\circ i

\displaystyle=\chi_{1_{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{f})\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(r_{\mathcal{C}})\circ i

\displaystyle=\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(f)}\circ\chi_{1_{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\mathbf{Tr}_{{\mathcal{V}}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(r_{\mathcal{C}})\circ i

\displaystyle=\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(f)}\circ\bar{i}\circ r_{\mathcal{V}}.

The third equality follows from involutivity of
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}
(Definition
2.20
),
and the final equality uses the unitality axiom

\chi_{1_{\mathcal{C}}}\circ\mathbf{Tr}(r_{\mathcal{C}})\circ i=\bar{i}\circ r_{\mathcal{V}}

from Definition
2.25
,
which holds by Proposition
2.26
.

Lemma 3.7
.

The state
{\mathcal{V}}(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(1_{\mathcal{C}}))\to\End_{\mathcal{V}}(1_{\mathcal{V}})\cong{\mathbb{C}}
given by
x\mapsto i^{\dagger}\circ x

corresponds to
\psi_{\mathcal{C}}:\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})\to{\mathbb{C}}
under the isomorphism (
16
).

Proof.

Fix
x\in{\mathcal{V}}(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(1_{\mathcal{C}}))
.
We then have

\psi_{\mathcal{C}}(\mate(x))=\langle\mate(x),\id_{1_{\mathcal{C}}}\rangle_{1_{\mathcal{C}}\to 1_{\mathcal{C}}}=\langle x,i\rangle_{1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(1_{\mathcal{C}})}=i^{\dagger}\circ x,

where the first equality holds by combining (
15
) with the definition of
\langle\cdot\,,\cdot\rangle
(Definition
2.1
), and the second equality is the
unitarity of the adjunction (
16
), using that
\mate(i)=\id_{1_{\mathcal{C}}}
.
∎

We will use the following lemma to get our equality of pairings in Proposition
3.9
below.

Lemma 3.8
.

Two maps
p,q:v\otimes\overline{v}\to 1_{\mathcal{V}}
are equal if and only if for all
u\in{\mathcal{V}}
and
f,g\in{\mathcal{V}}(u\to v)
,

p\circ(f\otimes\overline{g})\circ\coev_{u}=q\circ(f\otimes\overline{g})\circ\coev_{u}.

(17)

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}.

Now, by Lemma
3.7
,
i^{\dagger}\circ\eqref{eq:ToApplyidag}=\psi_{\mathcal{C}}(\eqref{eq:ToApplyPsiC})
. By (
15
) and the definition of
\langle\cdot\,,\cdot\rangle
,
this is equal to

\langle\mate(f),\mate(g)\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}(\Phi(v)\to c)}=\langle f,g\rangle_{{\mathcal{V}}(v\to\mathbf{Tr}(c))}=\tr_{\mathcal{V}}(fg^{\dagger})=\coev^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(c)}\circ(f\otimes\overline{g})\circ\coev_{v}.

Hence

i^{\dagger}\circ\eqref{eq:ToApplyidag}=\coev^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(c)}\circ(f\otimes\overline{g})\circ\coev_{v}\qquad\qquad\forall\,f,g:v\to\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(c).

The result follows by Lemma
3.8
.
∎

Remark 3.10
.

The problem of showing the pairing on the right hand side in the statement of Proposition
3.9
is non-degenerate was left open in
[
HPT16
, Rem. 5.4]
.
As it is equal to
\coev^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(c)}
(up to suppressing
\chi
), this open question is now resolved in the unitary setting.

3.4
Unitarity of the traciator

Suppose
({\mathcal{C}},\vee_{\mathcal{C}},\psi_{\mathcal{C}},\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}})
is a unitary module multitensor category over
{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{V}}
is the right unitary adjoint of
\Phi:{\mathcal{V}}\to{\mathcal{C}}
.
Recall that each object
\Phi(v)
comes with a unitary half-braiding
e_{\Phi(v),x}:\Phi(v)\otimes{x}\,\to\,{x}\otimes\Phi(v)
.
In this section, we explore an extra coherence between these unitary half-braidings and the involutive structure of the categorified trace.

Lemma 3.12
.

We have the following coherence between the half-braiding
e_{\Phi(v),\bullet}
and
\chi^{\Phi}_{v}
:

(\id_{\overline{b}}\otimes\chi^{\Phi}_{v})\circ e_{\Phi(\overline{v}),\overline{b}}=\big[\nu_{b,\Phi(v)}^{-1}\circ\overline{e^{-1}_{\Phi(v),b}}\circ\nu_{\Phi(v),b}\big]\circ(\chi^{\Phi}_{v}\otimes\id_{\overline{b}}).

Proof.

Letting
(\overline{\Phi(v)},e_{\overline{\Phi(v)},\bullet})
be the conjugate of
(\Phi(v),e_{\Phi(v),\bullet})
in
Z^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
, we have

e_{\overline{\Phi(v)},b}=\nu_{b,\Phi(v)}^{-1}\circ\overline{e^{-1}_{\Phi(v),b}}\circ\nu_{\Phi(v),b}
, so
the right hand side in the statement of the lemma simplifies to

e_{\overline{\Phi(v)},b}\circ(\chi^{\Phi}_{v}\otimes\id_{\overline{b}})
.
(Note that since the half-braiding is unitary, we have
\overline{e^{-1}_{\Phi(v),b}}=e^{\vee}_{\Phi(v),b}
.)
The result holds since
\chi^{\Phi}_{v}:\Phi(\overline{v})\to\overline{\Phi(v)}
is a morphism in
Z^{\dagger}({\mathcal{C}})
.
∎

The following lemma expresses the coherence from Lemma
3.12
in terms of traciators.

Lemma 3.13
.

We have the following compatibility of the tracitator with the involutive structure of
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}
:

\overline{\tau_{x,y}}\circ\chi_{x\otimes y}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu_{y,x})=\chi_{y\otimes x}\circ\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu_{x,y})\circ\tau_{\overline{x},\overline{y}}^{-1}

(22)

Proof.

We prove this equality after talking inverses on both sides, and after taking mates under the adjunction

{\mathcal{V}}\big(\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)}\to\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{y}\otimes\overline{x})\big)\cong{\mathcal{C}}\big(\Phi(\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)})\to\overline{y}\otimes\overline{x}\big).

The mate of the inverse of the left hand side of (
22
) is

\displaystyle\mate(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu_{y,x}^{-1})\circ\chi_{x\otimes y}^{-1}\circ\overline{\tau_{x,y}^{-1}})

\displaystyle=\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\mate(\chi_{x\otimes y}^{-1})\circ\Phi(\overline{\tau_{x,y}^{-1}})

\displaystyle=\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\varepsilon_{\overline{x\otimes y}}\circ\Phi(\chi_{x\otimes y}^{-1})\circ\Phi(\overline{\tau_{x,y}^{-1}})

\displaystyle=\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\overline{\varepsilon_{x\otimes y}}\circ\chi^{\Phi}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(x\otimes y)}\circ\Phi(\overline{\tau_{x,y}^{-1}})

\displaystyle=\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\overline{\varepsilon_{x\otimes y}}\circ\overline{\Phi(\tau_{x,y}^{-1})}\circ\chi^{\Phi}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)}

\displaystyle=\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\overline{\varepsilon_{x\otimes y}\circ\Phi(\tau_{x,y}^{-1})}\circ\chi^{\Phi}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)}

\displaystyle=\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\overline{\mate(\tau_{x,y}^{-1})}\circ\chi^{\Phi}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)}

where the third equality holds by the last equation in Proposition
2.21
.

The mate of the inverse of the right hand side of (
22
) is

\mate(\tau_{\overline{x},\overline{y}})\circ\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu_{x,y}^{-1}))\circ\Phi(\chi_{y\otimes x}^{-1})
.
Expanding, we get the map going right and then down in the pasting diagram below.
To save space, we omit tensor symbols and subscripts.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x)})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{y\cdot x}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{x}\cdot\overline{y}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x))}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x)})\cdot\overline{y}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{y\cdot x}))\cdot\overline{y}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{x}\cdot\overline{y}))\cdot\overline{y}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x))}\cdot\overline{y}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\Phi(\overline{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x)})\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{y\cdot x}))\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\overline{x}\cdot\overline{y}))\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y\cdot\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x))}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\overline{x}\cdot\overline{y}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x))\cdot y}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\overline{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\cdot x))}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\overline{y\cdot x}\cdot y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{y}\cdot\overline{x}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\chi^{-1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{\Phi}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\ev^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu^{-1}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\ev^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\ev^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\ev^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\chi^{-1})\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi^{\Phi}\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu^{-1}))\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e\cdot\id}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\chi^{\Phi}\cdot\id}
Prop.
2.21
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(\nu^{-1}))\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{e^{-1}}\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\ev}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{-1}\cdot\id}
Lem.
3.12
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\overline{\varepsilon}\cdot\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\cdot\nu^{-1}\cdot\id}

It remains to prove that the map going down and then right in the above pasting diagram is equal to
\nu_{y,x}^{-1}\circ\overline{\mate(\tau_{x,y}^{-1})}\circ\chi^{\Phi}_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)}
.
Equivalently, we must show that

\displaystyle\overline{\mate(\tau_{x,y}^{-1})}=\nu_{y,x}

\displaystyle\circ(\id_{\overline{y}\otimes\overline{x}}\otimes\ev_{y})\circ(\id_{\overline{y}}\otimes(\nu_{x,y}^{-1}\circ\overline{\varepsilon_{y\otimes x}})\otimes\id_{y})

\displaystyle\circ((\nu_{y,\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x))}^{-1}\circ\overline{e^{-1}_{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)),y}})\otimes\id_{y})\circ(\id_{\overline{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x))}}\otimes\ev_{y}^{\dagger}).

By the coherences for
(\overline{\,\cdot\,},\nu)
, the above equality is equivalent to

\displaystyle\mate(\tau_{x,y}^{-1})=(\coev_{y}^{\dagger}\otimes\id_{x\otimes y})

\displaystyle\circ(\id_{\overline{y}}\otimes\varepsilon_{y\otimes x}\otimes\id_{y})

\displaystyle\circ(\id_{\overline{y}}\otimes e^{-1}_{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x)),y})\circ(\coev_{y}\otimes\id_{\Phi(\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(y\otimes x))}),

which is exactly
[
HPT16
, Lem. 4.14]
.
∎

In Jones’ planar algebras
[
Jon21
]
, unitarity of the rotation plays a crucial
role.
Under the equivalence between anchored planar algebras and pivotal module tensor categories,
the analog of rotation is given by the traciator.
The next result says that traciators, and thus rotations in an anchored planar algebra, are unitary assuming sphericality.

Proposition 3.14
.

If the state
\psi_{\mathcal{C}}
is spherical, then the traciator
\tau_{a,b}
is unitary.

Proof.

Since
\tau_{a,b}
is invertible, it suffices to show that
\tau_{a,b}^{\dagger}\tau_{a,b}=\id_{\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(a\otimes b)}
.
Since
\tau^{\dagger}=\overline{\tau}^{\vee}
, by Lemma
3.13
(and suppressing various coherences) we have
\tau^{\dagger}=(\tau^{-1})^{\vee}
.
Thus:

\displaystyle\tau_{a,b}^{\dagger}\tau_{a,b}

4
Unitary anchored planar algebras

4.1
Planar algebras

We present here an abridged introduction to planar tangles, the planar operad, and planar algebras, and refer the reader to
[
HPT23b
, §2.1]
for an extended treatment.

An
planar tangle
consists of a collection of (round) parametrized disc
D_{1},\ldots,D_{n}
inside some biger parametrised disc
D_{0}
, along with a collection of non-intersecting paths in
D_{0}\setminus(D_{1}\cup\ldots\cup D_{k})
called
strings
that start and end at the boundary of one of the circles, or are themselves closed loops.
Here, a disc
D_{i}
is called
parametrised
if
D_{i}=\varphi_{i}({\mathbb{D}})
for some chosen affine linear maps
\varphi_{i}:{\mathbb{D}}\to D_{i}
from the standard unit disc.
The points
\varphi_{i}(1)\in\partial D_{i}
are called
anchor points
, and the strands are required to not start or end on the anchor points.
Here is an example of a planar tangle, where we have marked the anchor points in red:

2
1

There is a composition operation for planar tangles

S\circ_{i}T:=S\cup\phi_{i}(T)

when the number of external string boundary points of
T
agrees with the number of internal string boundary points in the
i
-th disk of
S
.
We shrink the tangle
T
, insert it into the
i
-th input disk of
S
using the map
\phi_{i}
, and match up the boundary points of the strings.
For an explicit example, see
[
HPT23b
, Ex. 2.2]
.

The collection of isotopy classes of planar tangles with the operation of tangle composition is called the
planar operad
.
A
planar algebra
is an algebra for this operad.
Unpacking, we have a vector space
{\mathcal{P}}[n]
for each
n\in{\mathbb{N}}_{\geq 0}
,
and each (isotopy class of) planar tangle
T
gives a linear map

Z(T):{\mathcal{P}}[n_{1}]\otimes\cdots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[n_{k}]\longrightarrow{\mathcal{P}}[n_{0}].

Here,
n_{i}
for
1\leq i\leq k
is the number of boundary points of strings on the
i
-th input disk of
T
, and
n_{0}
is the number of boundary points of strings on the output disk of
T
.
For future convenience, we abbreviate these properties by saying
T
has
type

(n_{1},\dots,n_{k};n_{0})
.

Given planar tangles
S,T
of types
(m_{1},\dots,m_{j};m_{0}),(n_{1},\dots,n_{k};n_{0})
respectively with
n_{0}=m_{i}
, composition of the linear maps
Z(S),Z(T)
must be compatible with composition of planar tangles:

Z(S\circ_{i}T)=Z(S)\circ(\id_{{\mathcal{P}}[m_{1}]\otimes\ldots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[m_{i-1}]}\otimes Z(T)\otimes\id_{{\mathcal{P}}[m_{i+1}]\otimes\ldots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[m_{j}]}).

We also require that the identity tangle must act as the identity linear map.
Finally, letting
T^{\sigma}
be the tangle obtained by renumbering the input disks of
T
by some permutation
\sigma
,
we should have
Z(T^{\sigma})=Z(T)\circ\sigma
(where we also use
\sigma
to denote the symmetric braiding of the vector spaces
{\mathcal{P}}[n_{i}]
corresponding to the permutation
\sigma
).

Remark 4.1
.

The notion of a planar algebra makes sense in any symmetric tensor category.

4.2

We present here an abridged introduction to the anchored planar operad and anchored planar algebras, and we refer the reader to
[

, §2.2]
for an extended treatment.

anchor line
which stays in
D_{0}\setminus\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\}
.
These anchor lines are transparent to the strings, but they may not intersect each other.

Like before, we say an anchored planar tangle
T
has
type

(n_{1},\dots,n_{k};n_{0})

if
T
has
k
input disks, the
i
-th input disk of
T
meets
n_{i}
string boundary points for
i\leq 1\leq k
, and the output disk of
T
meets
n_{0}
string boundary points.

The
anchored planar operad
is the collection of isotopy classes of anchored planar tangles, with the operation of tangle composition.
Here, given anchored planar tangles
S,T
of type
(m_{1},\dots,m_{j};m_{0}),(n_{1},\dots,n_{k};n_{0})
respectively with
n_{0}=m_{i}
, the composition operation
S\circ_{i}T
differs from the previous operation in that we must also give new anchor lines.
We do so by replacing the
i
-th anchor line of
T
by
k
parallel lines, and composing each one of them with the
i
-th anchor line of
S
,
as illustrated in the following picture:

(By

Definition 4.2
.

Let
({\mathcal{V}},\beta,\varphi^{\mathcal{V}})
be a braided pivotal tensor category.
An anchored planar algebra over
{\mathcal{V}}
is an algebra in
{\mathcal{V}}
over the anchored planar operad.
Unpacking, we have a sequence
{\mathcal{P}}=({\mathcal{P}}[n])_{n\geq 0}
of objects of
{\mathcal{V}}
, along with operations

Z(T):{\mathcal{P}}[n_{1}]\otimes\ldots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[n_{k}]\to{\mathcal{P}}[n_{0}]

for every isotopy class of anchored planar tangle
T
of type
(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k};n_{0})
,
subject to the following axioms:

•

(identity) the identity anchored tangle acts as the identity morphism

•

(composition) if
S
and
T
are anchored planar tangles of type
(m_{1},\ldots,m_{j};m_{0})
and
(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k};n_{0})
, and if
n_{0}=m_{i}
, then

Z(S\circ_{i}T)=Z(S)\circ(\id_{{\mathcal{P}}[m_{1}]\otimes\ldots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[m_{i-1}]}\otimes Z(T)\otimes\id_{{\mathcal{P}}[m_{i+1}]\otimes\ldots\otimes{\mathcal{P}}[m_{j}]})

the
n

box object
of the anchored planar algebra

.

Notation 4.3
.

In the sections below,
we use the notation of an anchored planar tangle
T
inserted into a coupon to denote the map
Z(T)
in
{\mathcal{V}}
afforded by an anchored planar algebra.
The strings in these diagrams are usually drawn horizontally for convenience, and we read them
left to right
.
For example:

Definition 4.4
.

A morphism
H:{\mathcal{P}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{P}}_{2}
of anchored planar algebras is
a sequence of morphisms
(H[n]:{\mathcal{P}}_{1}[n]\to{\mathcal{P}}_{2}[n])_{n\geq 0}
such that for every anchored planar tangle
T
of type
(n_{1},\dots,n_{k};n_{0})
,

H[n_{0}]\circ Z(T)=Z(T)\circ(H[n_{1}]\otimes\cdots\otimes H[n_{k}])
.

In this paper, we do not always assume our anchored planar algebras to be spherical.

Definition 4.6
.

A morphism
H:({\mathcal{P}}_{1},r^{1},\psi_{1})\to({\mathcal{P}}_{2},r^{2},\psi_{2})
of unitary anchored planar algebras is a morphism
H
of anchored planar algebras satisfying

\overline{H[n]}\circ r^{1}_{n}=r^{2}_{n}\circ H[n]
for all
n\geq 0
,
and

\psi_{1}=\psi_{2}\circ H[0]
.

When
{\mathcal{V}}={\sf Hilb_{fd}}
, the definition of unitary anchored planar algebra reduces to the definition of a unitary planar algebra (also known as a semisimple
\rm C^{*}
planar algebra) from
[
GMP+23
]
, but equipped with a faithful state. (The planar algebra of a bipartite graph
[
Jon00
]
is an example of a
\rm C^{*}
planar algebra that is naturally equipped wiht a faithful state.)

The following lemma is straightfoward and left to the reader.

Lemma 4.7
.

If a unitary anchored planar algebra is spherical, then for every
n\geq 0
we have

Proposition 4.8
.

Let
({\mathcal{P}},r,\psi_{\mathcal{P}})
be a spherical unitary anchored planar algebra.
Let
A
be an annular anchored planar tangle,
and denote the inside-out reflection by
A^{\dagger}
.
Then
Z(A)^{\dagger}=Z(A^{\dagger})
.

5
Extending the equivalence

We now prove Theorem
A
, extending the equivalence from
[
HPT23b
, Thm. A]
to an equivalence

\left\{\,\parbox{128.0374pt}{\rm Unitary anchored planar algebras in ${\mathcal{V}}$}\left\}\,\,\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{\,\parbox{184.9429pt}{\rm Pointed unitary module multitensor categories over ${\mathcal{V}}$}\,\right\}\right.\right.\!\!.

Recall that, by definition (see §
3.2
), a unitary module multitensor category comes with a state
\psi_{\mathcal{C}}
and requires that the
{\mathcal{V}}
-action
\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle Z}:{\mathcal{V}}\to Z^{{\dagger}}({\mathcal{C}})
is pivotal.

5.1
From unitary module tensor categories to unitary anchored planar algebras

Let
({\mathcal{C}},\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}},\vee_{\mathcal{C}},\psi_{\mathcal{C}})

be a pointed unitary module multitensor category over
{\mathcal{V}}
, with real generator
(x,r_{x})\in{\mathcal{C}}
,
and
\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}:{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{V}}
the unitary right adjoint of
\Phi=\Forget_{\mathcal{Z}}\circ\Phi^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{Z}}}:{\mathcal{V}}\to{\mathcal{C}}
.
We may then construct an ordinary anchored planar algebra, as in
[
HPT23b
, Thm. 5.1]
.
This anchored planar algebra is completely determined by the following information:

•

{\mathcal{P}}[n]:=\mathbf{Tr}_{\mathcal{V}}(x^{\otimes n})

•
